newsitem.title: USA: US dlr may stay "overvalued" until 2000 - Conf Board.
newsitem.headline: US dlr may stay "overvalued" until 2000 - Conf Board.

text.p: The dollar is in an extended period of overvaluation -- especially against the mark -- that may last until 2000, despite the U.S. currency's recent weakness, said a Conference Board report released on Tuesday.
"The recent drop in the dollar is more about decoupling than decline," said Gail Fosler, senior vice president and chief economist of The Conference Board.

"The dollar has moved up against the yen and the mark for most of the year," Fosler said. "Now the improving Japanese trade surplus and the politics that surround it are beginning to bite into the dollar's strength against the yen."
Fosler said the yen has seen its lows, but the mark has "significant" further declines ahead.
The analysis appears in the latest issue of Straight Talk, Fosler's newsletter prepared for associates of the Conference Board, a U.S.-based business research organization.
Specifically, the Conference Board forecast the dollar will likely rise to 1.85 marks by early 1998, with 2.0 marks a possibility during the year.
Although the dollar's strength versus the yen is capped by Japan's growing trade surplus, the dollar will remain above 120 yen for most of 1997 and 110 yen for 1998, the report said.
"The strength of the dollar arises from recent trends in world trade and finance and from economic and currency weakness abroad, particularly in Europe," Fosler said.
"The dollar strength will continue beyond the initial introduction of the Euro until the new currency becomes broadly used in transactions and in financial markets," she added.

The sharp rise in foreign direct investment in the developing countries has also provided support for the dollar, the report said. Foreign exchange reserves in developing countries, particularly in Asia, are overwhelmingly concentrated in dollars.

"While each of these trends alone are significant, together they constitute a critical mass that favors a strong dollar, particularly versus the deutschemark," the Conference Board chief economist said.

Fosler said the next few years do not constitute a new era in dollar valuation. But she added that the global economy has certainly entered an extended phase where structural forces will continue to increase the overall demand for dollars.

She noted the U.S. economy is slowing in the current quarter but said this is a pause, not a trend. The economy will reaccelerate in the second half of 1997 with higher rates and a stronger dollar, she said.
With industrial growth expected to increase at a 4.0 percent annual rate this year, exports should rise by about 8.0 percent and imports by about 7.0 percent, the report said.
A 10 percent rise in the dollar boosts import growth by about one percentage point and subtracts about the same amount from export growth, it said.

The report concluded that the appreciation in the dollar so far suggests the trade gap will widen throughout 1997, with imports climbing into the 9.0 percent range and exports slowing to a 7.0 percent to 8.0 percent rate by year's end.
